beats.lead: The popular version blames poisoned bread
beats.text: Historians doubt ergot. Dancing for days does not fit it.
beats.note: John Waller argues poisoned people would be unlikely to keep dancing for days, and ergot cannot explain outbreaks along the Rhine and Moselle.

beats.name: Frau Troffea
beats.role: Began dancing in a Strasbourg street on 14 July, with no music. Four of the six chronicle accounts name her.

beats.lead: The council's fix made it worse
beats.text: Later accounts say officials built stages and paid musicians. More people joined in.
beats.note: Onlookers read the spectacle as the anger of Saint Vitus. The council then tore the stages down and banned dancing and music.

beats.lead: The death toll is a claim, not a record
beats.text: The often repeated 15 deaths a day rests on later accounts.
beats.note: Contemporary Strasbourg sources do not mention deaths, and historians disagree on whether anyone died.

beats.text: The favoured explanation today is stress, not poison.

beats.line: Hardship can look like a spell.
